title: Your first project folder
promise: You're going to have a real project folder on your computer. It'll sit at a path, meaning an address, that won't give you trouble. Inside it'll have its README.md, its .gitignore, and its .env.example. And you'll be able to say out loud what every file in there is for.
why: Javi runs a physical therapy clinic in Getafe. He wanted a page so people could book appointments without calling. Over two afternoons, ChatGPT wrote him the fourteen files he needed. He saved them to his Desktop as they came in, mixed in with invoices and screenshots. By the third day he had three files named index.html, two folders named web, and no way to tell which one was the right one. He didn't get stuck coding: he got stuck because he never decided where his project lived.

theory.title: The folder doesn't hold your project: the folder IS your project
theory.text: A project isn't an idea with files scattered around it. It's a folder, and everything the project needs lives inside it. The test is simple. Copy that folder onto a USB stick and take it to another computer. If it works there, you had a project. If something gets left behind when you copy it, you didn't have a project. For example, an image that was in Downloads, or a text you had on the Desktop. Those are loose files that only knew each other by sight. This is exactly where the Desktop fails: the Desktop isn't a container, it's a table. Everything you leave on it lives together with your bank PDFs and your phone photos. And nothing tells you what belongs to what. The doubt that'll come up is: what if I need a photo I have in Downloads? The answer is always the same: you copy it inside the project folder. A file that's outside doesn't exist, as far as your project is concerned.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between a moving box, closed and labeled, and having your things scattered around the whole house. You grab the box and take it without thinking. With things scattered around, you always leave something behind in a drawer.
theory.example: Javi zipped his citas-fisio folder into a 380 KB ZIP and sent it to his nephew to take a look. His nephew opened it and everything was in there. While the project lived on the Desktop there was no way to send it: it was fourteen files mixed in with forty-one others.

theory.title: Where to put it: the address matters more than it seems
theory.text: Where you create the folder is a technical decision, even though it doesn't look like one. Three things are going to cause you problems. All three are invisible until they blow up. The first is the cloud. On most Windows and Mac machines today, the Desktop and Documents aren't actually inside your computer. They're synced with OneDrive or iCloud. That means a file can show up in the list without being truly downloaded. When a program tries to open it, it's going to find a gap. The second is accented letters and spaces inside the path, which is the folder's full address. Many tools swallow them fine. Others choke and give you back an error that doesn't mention the accent anywhere. The third only happens on Windows: there's an old 260-character limit on a file's full address. Projects nest folders inside folders cheerfully enough to eat through that limit sooner than you'd think. The fix for all three is the same and takes a minute. Create a folder called projects, lowercase, hanging directly off your user folder. And put all your projects there. And the question that follows is a good one: if I take it out of OneDrive, don't I lose my backup? Yes. That's why at the end of this lesson you duplicate the folder by hand. Later on GitHub will do that for you, and it also keeps every version, not just the last one.
theory.analogy: It's like setting up your workshop in the garage instead of in the hallway of your house. It fits in the hallway, but people pass through, everything gets moved around, and someone ends up walking off with a piece without meaning to.
theory.example: Compare these two addresses. C:\Users\Begoña\OneDrive\Desktop\My Web Page\ has four problems at once: an accented letter, a folder synced with the cloud, two spaces, and capital letters. C:\Users\bego\projects\citas-fisio\ has none of them, and takes up half the characters too.

theory.title: The map inside: what you'll find when you open it
theory.text: A project folder has three kinds of content. Learning to tell them apart saves you half the scares. The first is what you write: your code, your images, your README. It's the only irreplaceable part: if you lose it, it's gone. The second is what the machine writes on its own. That's where the node_modules folder and the package-lock.json file go. Also some folder called dist or .next, which will show up the day you start the project. All of that is heavy and generates itself. You can delete it without drama, because it comes back the same. And the third are the secrets: a single file with your keys, which should never leave your computer. Looking at that list, one doubt will come up: do you have to create all of that yourself? No. Out of the whole list you create three files and at most two folders. The rest shows up on its own once you install and start it up. The topmost folder, the one that contains all the others, is called the root. When someone tells you put it in the root, they mean right there, loose, not inside any subfolder. A project having few folders at the start doesn't mean it's half-done: it means it's clean.
theory.example:
citas-fisio/            <- the root: this folder IS the project
  README.md             <- you write this, today
  .gitignore            <- you write this, today
  .env.example           <- you write this, today
  .env.local             <- your real keys, never leaves here
  package.json           <- the project's shopping list
  package-lock.json      <- the machine writes this, don't touch it
  node_modules/           <- 287 MB of borrowed pieces, generates itself
  public/                <- the logo, the photos, the tab icon
  src/                    <- your real code

theory.title: File by file, what each one does
theory.text: README.md is a note you write to yourself: what this is, how to start it, and what you decided. The .md at the end means it's written with simple markup: hashes for headings and dashes for lists. That's why it reads well anywhere. package.json is the ID card and the shopping list at once. It says what the project's called, what borrowed pieces it needs, and what order it starts in. package-lock.json pins the exact version of each of those pieces, down to the last digit. It's what makes the project work tomorrow the same way it works today. Don't edit it or delete it. node_modules is the folder where the borrowed pieces get downloaded into. It's two or three hundred megs and tens of thousands of files you'll never open in your life. It regenerates entirely with a single command, so it's the only folder in the project you can delete without worry. .gitignore is a list of names that means this doesn't get copied or uploaded anywhere. node_modules and the secrets always go in there. .env.local holds your access keys for paid services. .env.example is its twin with the values erased. It's there so that in six months you remember what keys were needed. And it stops a key from ending up written somewhere that could get published. public/ is what gets served as-is: the logo, the photos, and the little tab icon. src/ is where the code that does something lives. If you ever open someone else's project and don't understand anything, start with the README and package.json. In five minutes you'll know what it is and how it starts up.
theory.example: Javi's website's package.json is fourteen lines, and one of them says "dev": "next dev". That means the command to start his project is npm run dev, and it's written there specifically so he doesn't have to remember it. His node_modules, in the folder next door, takes up 287 MB spread across about 41,000 files.

theory.title: The two tricks your computer plays on you without warning
theory.text: Windows and Mac come out of the box hiding two things from you, and both are going to bite you today. The first is the extension: those three or four letters after the last dot that tell the computer what type of file it is. You see a file that says README and it's actually called README.md. Or worse: it's called README.md.txt, because Notepad added the .txt on its own when saving. With that extra .txt, the file stops being what you think it is and no program recognizes it. The second is that they hide every file whose name starts with a dot. And it just so happens that two of your project's most important files start with a dot: .gitignore and .env.local. You'll create them, they'll disappear from view, and you'll think they didn't save. They're right there. Before you create anything, turn both things on: visible extensions and visible hidden files. They're two checkboxes: they don't break anything, they don't delete anything, and you can turn them off again whenever you want. And if you're on Mac, watch out for TextEdit. If you don't tell it to write plain text, it saves an .rtf. Underneath, that isn't plain text, even though it looks like it to you.
theory.analogy: It's like a closet that hides the bottom drawers so everything looks tidier. The catch is your house keys are stored down there.

theory.title: How everything gets named: lowercase, hyphens, and nothing else
theory.text: There's a single naming rule, and it applies to folders, files, and images. Everything lowercase, words separated by hyphens, no accents, no special characters, no spaces, no parentheses. It's not just fussiness from tidy people. It's that your computer and the server where your site will eventually live don't think the same way. The server is the internet computer that shows your page to everyone else. Your Windows or Mac treats Logo.png and logo.png as the same file. That server almost always runs Linux, a different operating system, and there they're two completely unrelated files. That's where the most frustrating bug of all comes from: on your laptop everything looks perfect, you publish, and the image doesn't show up. And with no message explaining why. Spaces cause a different kind of trouble. In an internet address they turn into an unreadable %20. And inside any command you type, they split the line in half. Parentheses like logo (1).png come from having downloaded the same thing twice. They're a sign you have duplicates you'll confuse someday. And here's a habit that'll pay off. When you put a date in a folder's name, write it backward: 2026-08-19, year, month, day. That way they sort themselves in chronological order. Written 08-19-2026, they don't sort, they get scrambled.
theory.example: Javi had the clinic's photo saved as Clinic Photo Getafe (1).PNG. On his laptop it looked fine. When he published the site, the broken-image gray box showed up. The name that works in both places is clinica-getafe.png.

tasks.title: Pick the project name and write it correctly
tasks.where: In a note on your phone or on paper, without opening any app yet
tasks.action: Write your project's name following three rules. Two words at most. All lowercase, joined by a hyphen. And it should describe WHAT it is, not what it's built with. citas-fisio, climbing-shop, or client-schedule work. my-react-project doesn't, because in a year the technology will be different and the name will lie. No accents, no special characters, no spaces, no capital letters. Under twenty characters. You're going to type this name a thousand times, so keep it short.
tasks.expect: A single line, something like citas-fisio. If it has a space, a capital letter, or an accent, rewrite it before moving on. If it's over twenty characters, trim it.
tasks.stuck: Describe your project in one sentence, out loud. Take the main noun and the sector or the place: booking an appointment at a physical therapy clinic gives you citas-fisio. That's good enough, don't hunt for the perfect name: this isn't the brand, it's a folder name.

tasks.title: Turn on extensions and hidden files
tasks.where: In Windows File Explorer or the Mac Finder
tasks.action: On Windows 11: press the Windows key and E together to open File Explorer. At the top, in the toolbar, click the View button. A menu drops down: go to Show and check both boxes, File name extensions and Hidden items. On Windows 10 it's the View tab at the top, and both checkboxes are right there. On Mac: open Finder and press Cmd + Shift + period to reveal hidden files. Then go to Finder, Settings (or Cmd + comma), the Advanced tab, and check Show all filename extensions. This doesn't delete or change anything, it just stops hiding things from you.
tasks.expect: Your usual files are now called invoice.pdf and photo.jpg, with the dot and letters at the end. And in your user folder new, dimmer-colored folders show up with odd names starting with a dot. That's the sign it worked.
tasks.stuck: If on Windows 11 you don't see the View button, the window is too narrow. The button is hidden behind the three dots. Widen the window. If on Mac you press Cmd + Shift + period and nothing happens, click inside a Finder window first, so it becomes the active window. Then try again.

tasks.title: Create the parent folder projects, outside the Desktop
tasks.where: In Windows File Explorer or the Mac Finder
tasks.action: On Windows: open File Explorer, click the address bar at the top, clear it, type C:\Users and press Enter. You'll see a folder with your username: go in. Right-click in an empty spot, New, Folder, and type projects in lowercase. If your username has an accent or a special character, better not hang the folder off there. Type C:\ in the address bar and create the projects folder there instead. Windows will ask for admin permission: click Continue. On Mac: Finder, Go menu, Home (or Cmd + Shift + H), right-click, New Folder, projects.
tasks.expect: The address bar reads C:\Users\yourname\projects or C:\projects. What matters is that the word OneDrive, Desktop, Documents, or Dropbox doesn't appear anywhere in that line.
tasks.stuck: When you go into your user folder, check if Desktop and Documents have a little cloud icon on them. If they do, they're synced: all the more reason not to create the project there. If Windows won't let you create anything in C:\ even with admin permission, use C:\Users\yourname\projects even if your name has an accent. It works in most cases, and you can always move the folder later.

tasks.title: Create the project folder and its minimal contents
tasks.where: Inside the projects folder you just created
tasks.action: Go into projects. Right-click, New, Folder, and type the name you decided on in task 1. Go into that new folder: it's empty, and that's how it should be. Create two more subfolders inside it, right-click, New, Folder: one called src and another called public, both lowercase. Don't create any other folder. Copy the full path that shows up in the address bar at the top and save it in a note. You'll need it in every lesson from here on.
tasks.expect: The address bar reads something like C:\Users\yourname\projects\citas-fisio, and inside you see two empty folders: public and src. Nothing else.
tasks.stuck: You might end up with a folder called New folder, because you clicked away before typing the name. Click it once and press F2 to rename it. If you created the folder in the wrong place, no problem: drag it into projects and it moves whole, with everything inside.

tasks.title: Ask the AI for YOUR project's map
tasks.where: In the ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini app, in a new conversation
tasks.action: Open a fresh, clean conversation, don't reuse an old one. Copy the whole prompt below, which is the text you're going to ask the AI. Paste it in the text box. Before sending it, fill in the three blanks between brackets. When it answers, don't close that conversation: you'll use it in the next three tasks.
tasks.prompt:
Act as the most experienced developer on the team, and treat me as what I am: someone who's never coded and who until today only ever used the Desktop.

My project is: [DESCRIBE IN TWO SENTENCES WHAT YOU WANT IT TO DO]. It's going to be used by: [WHO, AND HOW MANY PEOPLE PER MONTH]. I work on: [Windows 11 or macOS].

Draw me the folder and file tree this project will have once finished, in plain text, with the root's full path written at the very top.

Rules for your answer:
1. Mark with [ME] the files and folders I have to create by hand myself, and with [AUTO] the ones that appear on their own when installing or starting.
2. Next to each one, a line of fifteen words at most saying what it does, no jargon and nothing assumed.
3. Tell me which of all of them I should never touch, and what would happen if I did.
4. Tell me which one, if it leaks onto the internet, could cost me money, and how much.
5. Don't give me the contents of any file yet: today I just want the map.
6. If my description is too vague to decide the structure, ask me at most three questions before drawing anything.
tasks.expect: A tree of ten to twenty lines with the root at the very top. Most lines marked [AUTO] and only three or four marked [ME]. And point 4 has to mention the .env or .env.local file as the dangerous one.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you back a sixty-line tree with folders called tests, docs, ci, or config, reply: Trim it to the bare minimum needed for the first working version, twelve lines max, and remove anything it won't need in the first week.

tasks.title: Write your README.md and actually save it
tasks.where: In the same AI conversation, and then in Windows Notepad or Mac TextEdit
tasks.action: Send the prompt below. Once you have the text, copy it whole. On Windows: open Notepad and paste it. Go to File, Save as. Before anything else, change the Type dropdown from Text documents to All files. In Encoding pick UTF-8. Type README.md as the name and navigate to your project folder to save it there. On Mac: open TextEdit and go to Format, Make Plain Text (or Cmd + Shift + T). Paste the text and go to File, Save. Type README.md and uncheck the box that says If no extension is provided, use ".txt".
tasks.prompt:
Write me my project's README.md file.

Context, the tree you gave me before:
[PASTE THE TREE FROM THE PREVIOUS TASK HERE]

The project does: [ONE SENTENCE].

This README will be read by exactly one person: me, in six months, when I won't remember a single thing about what I did. Write it with that reader in mind and no one else.

Include these seven sections, in this order and with these exact headings:
1. What this is: two sentences, not a single technical term.
2. Who it's for and what problem it solves: two sentences.
3. How I start it on my computer: numbered steps, one per line, with the exact command in quotes wherever needed.
4. What I need installed beforehand: a list with the name and minimum version of each thing.
5. What files there are and what each one is for: one line per file.
6. What I should never upload to the internet: a short, blunt list.
7. Decisions I made and why: leave three blank bullet points for me to fill in by hand.

Write it in plain English and in Markdown format. Don't make up a single fact: if you're missing something to complete a section, write PENDING in capital letters right there and move on.
tasks.expect: A file named exactly README.md inside your project folder. Inside, the headings start with a hash, and the word PENDING shows up wherever the AI didn't have data. If File Explorer shows it as README.md, good; if it shows it as README.md.txt, bad.
tasks.stuck: If the file saved as README.md.txt, you didn't change Type to All files. Click it, press F2, and remove the .txt at the end. Windows will ask if you're sure about changing the extension: say yes. If you don't see the .txt anywhere, you skipped task 2. Go back and turn on extensions.

tasks.title: Create the .gitignore, the list of what doesn't leave here
tasks.where: In the AI conversation, and then in the same text editor
tasks.action: Send the prompt below. Copy only what comes inside the code block. Save it in the project's root, next to the README, named .gitignore: with the dot in front and nothing after it. Read the table it gives you underneath before moving on to anything else. Understanding those fifteen lines means understanding what's trash and what's yours.
tasks.prompt:
I need the contents of my project's .gitignore file.

My project is: [DESCRIBE IT IN ONE SENTENCE, AND IF YOU KNOW WHAT IT'S BUILT WITH, SAY SO; IF YOU DON'T KNOW, SAY YOU DON'T KNOW]. I work on: [Windows or Mac].

First give me the file's contents inside a code block, ready to copy and paste, with no explanations inside the block except short comments grouping the lines.

Then, outside the block, make me a two-column table: on the left, the line from the file; on the right, exactly what it's excluding and why it makes sense to exclude it, in plain language.

Make sure to include:
- The folder where the borrowed pieces get downloaded into.
- Every secrets file, in all its variants.
- The junk my operating system generates (Thumbs.db on Windows, .DS_Store on Mac).

Don't include rules for technologies I'm not using: I don't want a two-hundred-line file copied from a generic template.
tasks.expect: A .gitignore file of fifteen to thirty lines in the project's root. It absolutely has to include node_modules, .env, and .env.local. If you turned on hidden files, you'll see it in File Explorer with a slightly dimmer icon than the rest.
tasks.stuck: Windows won't let you name a file starting with a dot: it'll tell you that you need to type a file name. The trick is to type .gitignore. with a dot at the end too, and press Enter. Windows strips the trailing dot and leaves you the right name. The other way is to save it from Notepad typing the name in quotes: ".gitignore".

tasks.title: Separate the secrets: .env.example and .env.local
tasks.where: In the AI conversation, and then in the text editor
tasks.action: Send the prompt below. Save what it gives you as .env.example in the project's root, using the same leading-dot trick. And create an empty file next to it called .env.local. That's the one that'll carry the real keys the day you have them. And it's the one that never, under any circumstances, leaves your computer. It doesn't get copied, doesn't get emailed, doesn't get pasted into a public chat, and doesn't get uploaded anywhere. Serious warning, with numbers behind it. There are documented invoices of hundreds of euros generated in a single night. A paid service's key published by mistake in a public repository gets found by automated bots within minutes. A public repository is a code folder visible to the whole internet. Revoking a leaked key, meaning canceling it, is free. Paying for someone else's usage isn't.
tasks.prompt:
Explain, for someone who's never coded, the .env.local and .env.example file pair in my project: why there are two, which one gets saved, and which one gets shared.

My project is going to connect to: [LIST THE SERVICES YOU KNOW: OpenAI, Stripe, a database, an email service... If you don't know any yet, say you don't know].

Give me, in this order:
1. The exact contents of .env.example, with variable names in capital letters and empty values or an obviously fake example like put-your-key-here.
2. One line per variable saying what it is and on what website and exact menu that key is obtained.
3. How much money, in dollars, leaking each of those keys could cost me, and which is the worst one of all.
4. What I need to do step by step if a key ever leaks: in what order I revoke it, regenerate it, and check the usage.

Don't write any real key or any made-up one that could look real.
tasks.expect: An .env.example file in the root with lines like OPENAI_API_KEY=put-your-key-here, and an empty .env.local next to it. And in the AI's answer, stated in plain terms, that .env.local never gets uploaded anywhere.
tasks.stuck: If you don't yet know what services your project will connect to, create the .env.example with a single example line. Come back to this task once you know. Don't leave it for the end, because the end is exactly when these mistakes happen. And check one thing before moving on: open the .env.example and make sure there's no real key in there.

tasks.title: Run the moving test
tasks.where: In File Explorer or Finder, then in the AI app
tasks.action: Right-click on your project folder and choose Compress to ZIP file (Windows 11) or Compress (Mac). Look at the size of the ZIP that got created: today it should weigh kilobytes, not megabytes. Then you have two options. You can type out by hand in the chat the list of what's inside your folder. That's eight or nine lines and takes a minute. Or you can take a screenshot with Windows + Shift + S and paste it into the conversation. With one of the two done, send the prompt below.
tasks.prompt:
I'm giving you the complete contents of my project folder, exactly as I see them in File Explorer:

[PASTE THE LIST HERE OR ATTACH THE SCREENSHOT]

Act as someone opening this folder for the first time, who doesn't know me at all and can't ask me anything. Tell me:
1. What do you think this project does? Answer only with what you can figure out from what you see, not from what I've told you before.
2. What file would you expect to find here that isn't there?
3. Is there anything that shouldn't be here: system junk, a stray copy, a duplicate file, or a secret in plain sight?
4. Is any name poorly chosen, with capital letters, accents, spaces, or not descriptive enough? Tell me the new name you'd give it.
5. Rate how understandable this folder is to an outsider from 1 to 10, and tell me the single thing that would raise that score the most.

Be hard on me. I'd rather you point out five problems now, while nothing's been built on top of it yet, than tell me everything's great.
tasks.expect: A ZIP under a megabyte, and an answer pointing out at least one thing to fix. If the AI tells you everything's perfect, push back once: Give me three concrete issues, even small ones.
tasks.stuck: If the ZIP weighs 200 MB or more, node_modules is already in there. You haven't done anything wrong. But to send the folder to someone, take that folder out or just delete it. It regenerates entirely with a single command and none of your own stuff gets lost.

tasks.title: Duplicate the folder as a dated backup
tasks.where: In Windows File Explorer or the Mac Finder
tasks.action: Right-click on the project folder, choose Copy, and paste it inside the same projects folder. You'll end up with something like citas-fisio - copy. Rename it (F2 on Windows, Enter on Mac) to citas-fisio-2026-08-19, with today's date in year-month-day format. That copy never gets touched again: it's your clean starting point. Repeat this move every time you're about to make a big change, until you learn to use GitHub and it stops being necessary. Warning: this protects you from breaking something, not from deleting it. If you send the folder to the trash and empty it, it's not coming back.
tasks.expect: Two sibling folders inside projects: citas-fisio and citas-fisio-2026-08-19, both with exactly the same thing inside.
tasks.stuck: If Windows tells you the file is in use and won't let you copy or rename it, close Notepad. And close any other program with a file from inside it open. If you pile up a lot of dated copies and your view gets cluttered, don't delete them yet. Keep the first one and the last two, and drag the rest into a subfolder called copies.

matters: The path where the project lives: no accents, no special characters, no spaces, and outside OneDrive or iCloud. If you choose it badly, the errors you get in two weeks won't mention the path anywhere. And you'll waste afternoons hunting for a bug in the code that isn't in the code.

Having secrets live in a separate file, and having that file written into .gitignore from day one. Not from the day you get real keys. It's the only thing in this lesson measured in dollars. A leaked key gets found by bots in minutes, and you're the one who pays the usage.

The README written on day one, not on the last day. Written today it costs you five minutes, and the AI does almost all the work. Written six months from now it costs you a whole afternoon of archaeology, trying to remember why you did things that way.

Names in lowercase and with hyphens, images included. It's what separates your site working on your computer from working on the internet. A capitalization mistake is the worst kind of bug there is: it gives no error message, the image just doesn't show up.
ignore: Git and GitHub. Today you just need the .gitignore file to exist and to know what's in it. Understanding why it's called that and what it's really for has its own lesson, and jumping ahead gains nothing.

What's inside node_modules. It's tens of thousands of files you'll never open, not now and not five years from now doing this. All you need to know is that it deletes without fear and comes back the same.

Choosing the definitive editor among VS Code, Cursor, Zed, or anything else. Today's folder gets fully built with File Explorer and Notepad. And choosing an editor with judgment is much easier once you already have a project to open with it.
canDo: Draw you the folder and file tree tailored to what you describe. And explain what every line is for, without you having to look it up on your own.
Write out the README.md, .gitignore, and .env.example whole and ready to copy. The content is adapted to your project, not a generic template.
Look at the list of what's in your folder, if you paste it. And tell you what's missing, what's extra, what's duplicated, and what's poorly named.
Translate any error like cannot find module or ENOENT into plain English for you. It almost always means a file isn't where the program expected to find it.
cantDo: Create folders or files on your hard drive from the ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini text box. There the AI writes the text and you save it by hand. The tools that do write directly onto your computer are others (Claude Code, Cursor, the Gemini console). And they come later.

See what you actually have on your computer. If you don't paste it the list or a screenshot, anything it tells you about your folder is being imagined. And it'll do it with total confidence and very polished writing.
Recover a file you deleted or a key you lost. A deleted .env.local doesn't get rebuilt by writing: you have to go into each service's website and generate new keys.
Know whether your Desktop is synced with OneDrive, whether your username has an accent, or how much your folder weighs. You check that yourself in the address bar and properties, and then tell it.
words: Folder
A drawer inside the computer where you put things, and inside which more drawers fit. When you see it written directory, it's exactly the same thing said in an older way.
Path

A folder's complete address written out in full, from the drive down to it, like a home address with street, number, and floor. On Windows the parts are separated by backslashes, and on Mac by forward slashes.
Root
The topmost folder of your project, the one that contains all the others. When someone tells you put it in the root, they mean right there, loose, not inside anything.
Extension
The three or four letters after a file name's last dot. It's what tells the computer what kind of thing it is and which program has to open it with.
README
A text file where you write the explanations of your project for yourself. It's called that, read-me in English, because it's the first thing anyone opens when they land in the folder.
Markdown
A way of writing text with very simple markup: hashes before headings and dashes before lists. It reads fine as-is, and many websites already display it formatted. Files written this way end in .md.
Dependency
A piece of program built by someone else that your project uses borrowed instead of writing it from scratch. A normal project uses hundreds.
node_modules

The folder where all those borrowed pieces get downloaded into. It's hundreds of megs and a single command creates it on its own. Don't touch it, don't copy it, don't send it to anyone. You can delete it without worry, since it comes back the same.
Environment variable
A piece of data your program needs but that you don't want written inside it: a password, a payment key, a server's address. It lives in a separate file that never leaves your computer.
kebab-case
The habit of writing names all in lowercase with hyphens where spaces would go: citas-fisio, store-logo.png. It's called that because the words end up skewered like meat on a kebab.
